docs.title: History of Entrepreneurship and Tech Innovation
Vision, Mission, and Strategic Planning
docs.text:
• Startups are special
  • Small: 3-10 people
  • Nimble: like the Navy Seals, no committee
  • Un-constrained: there are no sacred cows
  • Courages: startups take risks, big companies found something that works and don't want to change

  • Innovative: small set of people starting with a blank slate can come up with something completely new

  • Fragile: a big company can easily crash a large company

  • Big-company vs startup

  • In a big company: responsibility diffuse, everyone has a little corner

  • In a startup: everyone feels responsible

  • In a big company: you must defend your cash cows

  • In a startup: you must put everything on the line

  • In a big company: incremental improvements to the working product

  • In a startup: innovate or die

  • In a big company: management is important

  • In a startup: management is not necessary (everyone knows what everyone is doing)

  • In a big company: default alive (if they don't do anything, they survive)

  • In a startup: default dead (everyone loses their job if startup doesn't innovate)

  • Why are startups so valuable?

  • Most economic growth comes from innovation
  • Most innovation comes from startups
  • Many Google products came from acquisition
  • DoubleClick
  • YouTube
  • Android

  • Google Maps

  • In a world of declining growth and interest rates, innovation is extremely valuable

  • How much percent return I will give you if you take my money and do something with it
  • It is a measure of how productive can be to loan out money

  • How many good ideas vs how many money

    • Right now there is a lot of money, but few ideas

  • In the last 800 years nominal interest rates have consistently going down (with cycles) but the trend is from 15% to 0%

  • US VC investments went from $50b in 2012 to $300b in 2022 (6x in 10 years)

  • The seed round went from $0.5m to $2.5m

  • If you are successful at a startup, the rewards are immense

  • But you probably won't be successful (and that's ok)

  • 5 big steps to build a startup

  • Learn the culture, products, and history of the sector
  • Find great co-founders and team
  • Come up with a great idea
  • Validate that the idea is great

  • Raise money for it

  • Step 1: Learn!

  • Before building anything learn as much as possible
  • Talk to people
  • Join a web3 startup
  • It's the best education you can get
  • Read, play, go to meet-ups and hackathons
  • Be technical

// From /Users/saggese/src/notes1/notes/IN_PROGRESS.book.work.2011.Osterwalder.Business_model_generation.txt

  • Value Proposition: Definition
  • The Value Proposition is the reason why customers turn to one company over another
  • VP solves a customer problem and satisfies a customer need

  • Product / service catering to a specific Customer Segment

  • Newness

  • VP can satisfy a new set of needs that customers previously didn't perceive
  • E.g., technology related

  • E.g., cellphones created a new industry around mobile communication

  • Performance

  • Improving product and service performance is a common way to create value

  • E.g., PC sector (more powerful machines, more disk storage, better graphics)

  • Customization

  • Tailor products and services to specific needs of Customer Segments / individual customers

  • E.g., mass customization

  • Getting the job done

  • E.g., airlines relying on manufacturers of jet engines, so they can focus on running airlines

  • Design

  • A product may stand out because of superior design
  • It might be difficult to measure

  • E.g., fashion industry, consumer electronics

  • Brand / status

  • Customers may find value in the act of using and displaying a specific brand
  • E.g., wearing a Rolex watch signifies wealth

  • E.g., skateboarders can wear the latest brands to show that they are "in"

  • Price

  • Offering similar value at a lower price

  • E.g., no-frills airline (Southwest) enable low-cost air travel

  • Cost reduction

  • Helping customers reduce costs creates value

  • Risk reduction

  • Customers value reducing risks when purchasing products or services
  • E.g., one-year guarantee
  • E.g., service-level guarantee in outsourced IT services

docs.title: Idea Generation and Validation Process
docs.text:
• Ideas
  • Ideas should not be safeguarded, they are not like secret jewels
  • You should tell everyone about your idea to understand which one is good
  • Have lots of ideas and talk about them

  • You need to iterate on the idea

  • There are two ways to find an idea

  • Top down ideation

  • Look at the industry, what are the biggest problems in the industry?
  • E.g., blockchain privacy, transaction monitoring, tax compliance
  • What is the total addressable market (TAM) for each problem?
  • What is the best possible outcome?
  • Maybe the only lesson to learn is when the TAM is too small
  • How crowded is the area?
  • Are there recent innovations that change the market structure?
  • E.g., zero-knowledge proofs
  • Read the prior art, get in touch with people
  • For ideas that require behavioral change, TAM is likely a futile exercise
  • Airbnb: "How many people will decide to stay in somebody else's house?"
  • Uber
  • Twitter is about talking with strangers
  • Behaviors change but that's difficult
  • Use your judgement, napkin math

  • How many piano tuners there are in Chicago?

  • Bottoms up ideation

  • What's the area you know best? What can I do?
  • If you don't know any area well, then spend time in it
  • What feels for me like me the biggest pain point?
  • You use your knowledge, your network, your relationships, distribution

  • Use your unfair edge

  • The risk is to over-optimization because you know what you like

  • What makes a good ideas?

  • A good idea solves a big, clearly articulable problem

  • Big: solving a small problem becomes a feature in somebody else product

  • Articulable: if you cannot define exactly the problem you are solving, but you think "this is really cool and people will like it"
  • E.g., "this is great since it's decentralized"

  • "Create a website that allows to showcase NFTs in a shareable way"

  • A good idea is defensible (it posses a moat)

  • When you solve a problem, you want to be the one that capitalizes on your solution

  • A good idea is easy to explain

  • If you can't explain, either it's not a good idea or you don't understand it

  • A good idea is a well-defined customer / user

  • A good idea has a "why now?"

  • Why doesn't this great solution already exist?

  • "If this was a good idea, somebody else would have built it" (like the Efficient Market Hypothesis)
  • Sometimes you need a stroke of insights
  • The most common cause for failing startups is founder breakup, nobody wants what you are building (this should be the default hypothesis)
  • Why now?
  • Nobody has my background and you need that to solve this problem
  • Crypto really grew in the last few years and now people need custodial services

  • Academic papers have been written and we made a product out of them

  • Good idea has a strong business model

  • High margin

  • Strong capture value
  • E.g., Linux created tons of value but didn't capture it

  • Music used to capture tons of value in the 90s (when you bought a CD), now with streaming has very low value capture (music is almost free)

  • Competition is inevitable

  • You don't have competition only if your idea is a bad one
  • If your competition has lock-in on the industry (e.g., distribution channels, exclusive contracts) that's a problem, if it's a startup go for it

  • You want to have a bias for markets that are not super crowded

  • Often it makes sense to start targeting a small population, even if the TAM is big

  • You want to build a product that people love than people like

  • You need to validate your idea

  • How do you know know if your idea is good?
  • You can't solve this problem by thinking about it in a dark room

  • You need external feedback

  • Who will use your product?

  • Define your user
  • Talk to people
  • Interview customers
  • Understand how they feel about this problem
  • How are they solving the problem today?
  • Know what other products they use, where they fall short

  • If there is no solution they are using, probably there is no problem!

  • "Would you use this if I built it?"

  • The answer is usually yes (since people tell you what you want to hear, and people want to be nice in a survey)

  • The answer is yes only if they actually pay for it ("would you pre-pay for it?")

  • Figure out their pain points

  • Your first idea is usually not perfect

  • It's ok to pivot: it happens all the time, e.g.,
  • Mt. Gox was a platform for Magic the Gathering cards
  • Coinbase was a Bitcoin wallet
  • Circle originally a P2P payments product (like CashApp)
  • OpenSea was WifiCoin (pay other people's wifi with crypto)
  • DYdX (derivatives) was a web3 search engine
  • Keep in mind the possibility of a pivot

  • Have a strong bias toward reversible decisions

  • The first idea gives you insights into the right way to solve a problem

  • Ideate quickly
  • Build quickly

  • Disprove assumptions quickly

  • Do not hide your idea

  • Talk to everyone

  • Customer Segments
  • No company can survive without customers
  • A company may group customers into distinct segments with common needs and behaviors
  • Justify a distinct offer
  • Reached through different Distribution Channels
  • Require different types of relationships
  • Have different profitability

  • A business model is designed around a strong understanding of specific customer needs

  • Mass market

  • A large group of customers with broadly similar needs and problems

  • E.g., in consumer electronics

  • Niche market

  • Specific, specialized Customer Segment

  • E.g. car part manufacturers depend on specific automobile manufacturers

  • Segmented

  • Customer segmented with slightly different needs and problems
  • E.g., a bank can distinguish customers worth up $100k and affluent clients worth more than $1M

  • E.g., a manufacturing solutions company targeting 3 CS, i.e., watch industry, medical industry, industrial automation sectors

  • Diversified

  • Serve unrelated Customer Segments with very different needs and problems

  • E.g., Amazon has retail business and cloud computing services (catering to Web companies with a totally different Value Proposition)

  • Multi-sided markets

  • Serve two or more interdependent Customer Segments
  • E.g., a credit card company needs credit card holders and merchants that accept credit cards
  • E.g., a company selling newspapers need reader base and advertisers

docs.title: User Research and Market Understanding
docs.text:
• More on a solving a problem
  • You are in trouble if you can't articulate an answer to the 2 questions:
  • Why will users use this product?
  • What problem does it solve? For whom?
  • Think in terms of a target customer
  • E.g., a customer that day trades NFTs, "Nathan lives in Virginia, has disposable income, every day he checks Reddit"

  • Make your product delightful for that user

  • How bad is the problem?

  • Is this a "nice-to-have" or a "must-have"?

  • Does it save costs or increase revenue?

  • Common ideation mistakes

  • Building for customers who don't exist yet
  • Almost always a mistake
  • Without real customers you don't get feedback (which kills startups), without feedback
  • Solving yesterday's problems, rather than tomorrow's problems
  • By the time you solve the problem it's going to be way to late
  • E.g., "build a platform for better ICOs", but ICOs were a thing of 2020 and nobody is doing ICOs in 2023
  • Building for crypto influencers
  • People of Twitter complain about "why there isn't XYZ?"
  • He is famous

  • I'm going to build XYZ

  • Are you building the right thing?

  • Build a proof of concept
  • Show it off online or at a hackathon
  • Many crypto projects were built without funding, hacked together
  • E.g., Uniswap, 1Inch

  • Can be reached through different Distribution Channels
  • Require different types of relationships

  • Products are usually standardized rather than customized
  • Focuses on high sales volume and low cost per unit

  • Diversified Customer Segments

  • Serve unrelated Customer Segments with very different needs and problems

  • E.g., Amazon has retail business and cloud computing services (catering to Web companies with a totally different Value Proposition)

  • Multi-sided markets

  • Serve two or more interdependent Customer Segments
  • E.g., a credit card company needs credit card holders and merchants that accept credit cards
  • E.g., a company selling newspapers need reader base and advertisers

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
* - Channels allow companies to communicate with and reach its Customer Segments to deliver a Value Proposition - Raise awareness among customers about a company's products and services - Allow customers to purchase products and services - Deliver Value Proposition to customers - Provide post-purchase customer support

  • Channel phases
  • Awareness
  • Raise customers' awareness about company's products and services
  • Evaluation
  • Help customers evaluate a company's Value Propositions
  • Purchase
  • Allow customers to purchase products and services
  • Delivery
  • Deliver value proposition to customers
  • After sales

  • Provide post-purchase customer support

  • Channel types

  • Owned channels
  • E.g., in-house sales force, web site
  • Higher margins but costly to put in place
  • Indirect
  • E.g., retail stores owned or operated by the company
  • Partner
  • E.g., wholesale distribution, retail
  • Lower margins but expand reach through partner strengths

docs.title: Customer relationships
docs.text:
• Company establish different types of relationships with Customer Segments
  • Customer acquisition
  • Customer retention

  • Boosting sales

  • Personal assistance

  • Human customer representative during the sales or after the purchase

  • E.g., point of sale, call centers, emails

  • Dedicated personal assistance

  • E.g., in private banking services for high net worth individuals

  • E.g., account managers maintaining personal relationships with important customers

  • Self-service

  • Provide necessary means for customers to hep themselves

  • Automated services

  • Mix customer self-service with automated processes

  • E.g., online profile allow to access customized services (e.g., recommendations)

  • Communities

  • Companies maintain online communities to exchange knowledge and solve users' problems

  • Co-creation

  • Companies invite customers to write reviews creating value for other customers (e.g., Amazon)
  • Engage customers to design new products
  • Solicit customers to create content (e.g., YouTube.com)

docs.title: Revenue Streams
docs.text:
* - For what value a Customer Segment is truly willing to pay? - Revenue Streams can have different pricing mechanisms (e.g., fixed list price, bargaining, auctioning, volume dependent, market dependent) - One-time payments vs ongoing payments

  • Asset sale

  • Sell ownership of a product

  • Usage fee

  • The more a service is used, the more the customer pays
  • E.g., number of minutes spent on the phone

  • E.g., a hotel charges by number of nights in a room

  • Subscription fee

  • Sell continuous access to a service

  • E.g., monthly subscription to a gym or to a web-based game

  • Lending / renting / leasing

  • Temporarily granting rights to use an asset for a fixed period

  • E.g., car rental

  • Licensing

  • Give customers permission to use intellectual property in exchange for a licensing fees

  • E.g., patent / copyright in media industry and technology

  • Brokerage fees

  • Intermediation services performed on behalf of multiple parties
  • E.g., credit card providers charge a percentage of transaction value

  • E.g., real estate agents earn a commission when matching buyers and sellers

  • Advertising

  • Fees for advertising product, service, or brand
  • E.g., media industry

docs.title: Pricing mechanisms
docs.text:
• List price

  • Fixed prices for products and services

  • Product feature dependent

  • Price depends on the number or quality of Value Proposition features

  • Customer segment dependent

  • Price depends on the type and characteristics of a Customer Segment

  • Volume dependent

  • Prices is function of the quantity purchased

  • Negotiation / bargaining

  • Price negotiated between partners (with different negotiation power / skills)

  • Yield management

  • Price depends on inventory

  • E.g., hotel rooms, airlines seats

  • Optimization

  • E.g., Blu-ray is a disc format developed by consumer electronic manufacturers, which then compute in selling their own Blu-ray products
  • Acquisition of particular resources and activities
  • Few companies own all the resources or perform all the activities required in their business model
  • Rather they rely on other firms to acquire knowledge, licenses, access to customers

docs.title: Cost Structure
docs.text:
• Business models incur in costs, e.g.,
  • Creating and delivering value
  • Maintaining Customer Relationships
  • Generating revenues
  • Costs should be minimized in every business model

  • Some business models are more sensitive to costs than others

  • Cost-driven companies

  • Create the leanest possible Cost Structure, using low-price Value Proposition, maximum automation, outsourcing

  • E.g., no-frills airlines (e.g., Southwest)

  • Value-driven companies

  • Some companies are less concerned with cost implication and focus on value creation

  • E.g., luxury hotels

  • Characteristics of cost structures

  • Fixed costs
  • Costs don't change despite volume of goods / services produced
  • E.g., salaries, rents
  • Variable costs
  • Costs that vary proportionally with the volume of goods / services produced
  • E.g., music festivals have high variable costs
  • Economies of scale
  • Cost advantages that a business enjoys as its output expands
  • Economies of scope
  • Cost advantages that a business enjoys due to a larger scope of operations
  • E.g., the same distribution channels and marketing can support multiple products

Competitive Analysis & Positioning (SWOT, differentiation)
docs.text:
• More on value capture
  • You should not stress out value capture in the beginning
  • The amount of value you capture is proportional to the amount of value you create
  • You need to pass some of the value to your customer

  • If your product saves people \$100, but it costs \$100 then your customers are indifferent

  • Tokens can capture value in many ways (discussed later)

  • There are many pricing models:
  • Value pricing
    • Best approach
    • Estimate how much value your are creating for your customers and charge a part of that (e.g., 50-80%)
  • Transaction pricing
    • Every time you make a transaction, I get a cut of it
    • E.g., financial exchange
  • Recurring revenues
    • E.g., there is a data service and you get a value out of it so you pay by seat
    • Some customers are getting a lot of value, others are getting small value
    • You don't know who is making money so you can't charge it
    • That's why people have multiple price tiers

  • Services

    • Somebody is paying you for doing something
    • E.g., a plumber charging for time and materials

  • Commodity pricing

  • The service becomes "cost + epsilon"
  • E.g., consulting
  • Price competition brings down the price to raw materials and wages
  • Even if you are creating value, you are not capturing it

  • This is the best situation for customers

  • E.g., the Internet creates tons of value but you almost don't pay for it

  • Internet is a commodity (like water)

  • 5 ways to build a $100m business

  • Hunt for 10,000 flies that pay you $10
  • Photoshop charges \$100 and need \$1m
  • Greenhouse, Salesforce (enterprise software): $100k people pay $1000
  • Big game hunting

  • Elephant hunting (e.g., Palantir): each customer pays $100,000k

  • More on defensibility

  • Competitors cannot easily enter the market or overtake your market share
  • E.g., network effect
  • E.g., Facebook, Ethereum, Binance

  • The platform that everybody uses is difficult to disrupt

  • Other sources of defensibility

  • Economy of scale
    • The R&D dept doesn't need to grow if you grow
  • Pricing power
    • You have the ability to squeeze your supplier, like others can't
  • First mover advantage
    • You are the first one to do something, so you build the relationships
  • Access to capital
    • Lots of business need working capital so they need to borrow money
    • It's easier for you to raise or borrow money (maybe because you have a great pedigree)
    • If you have strong reputation or pedigree
  • Access to talent

  • Execution

    • It is the weakest
    • You can outrun your competitors
    • I have ability to build faster, ship faster than my competitors

  • Market structure

  • In almost all industries there are companies with certain characteristics
  • Some companies own the user relationship
    • High value capture
    • Network effects
    • Brand
  • Some companies are integrators (they put things together)
    • Low value capture (they get squeezed between the extremes)
    • Few moats

  • Some companies own the tech platform

    • High value capture
    • High switching costs
    • Economies of scale
    • Technical barriers

  • E.g., mobile

  • (Facebook, Apple) <-> Motorola <-> ARM
  • E.g., auto
  • Tesla <-> Modine <-> Mobileye
  • E.g., streaming
  • Netflix <-> Starz <-> AWS
  • E.g., computers

  • Microsoft <-> Acer <-> Intel

  • Even if you have the best content but you need to go through Netflix to distribute it

  • Netflix wants to commoditize everyone else
  • For this reason Disney started Disney+

  • AWS copies / adopts open source projects and puts them on their platform

  • Same phenomenon also in crypto

  • Own user relationship: Coinbase, Binance
  • Integrators: protocols (e.g., Uniswap)

  • Tech platform: Ethereum, Bitcoin

  • Everyone tries to move up the curve

  • Coinmarketcap and Coingecko start adding the buy button to allow trading
  • Polkadot compete with other blockchains to have people build on top of them
  • Uniswap builds a web interface to interact with users

  • Binance builds a BNB chain

  • At the bottom of the curve, your users is who is close to you

docs.text:
• Product
  • A tool or utility that solves a need
  • Sometimes the problem solves a problem that it is different than what it is actually solving
  • E.g., Facebook "make the world more connected" vs "need of humans to show off" and "do something when you are bored"
  • The best product usually doesn't win
  • What's difficult is how to acquire users

  • Markets are pretty unfair because there are companies with unfair advantages and are willing to use it

  • Needs

  • You need to understand which of the 7 deadly sins your product is catering to

  • There are few human drivers

  • Lust (vs chastity)
  • Gluttony (vs temperance)
  • Greed (vs generosity)
  • Sloth (vs diligence)
  • Wrath (vs patience)
  • Envy (vs gratitude)
  • Pride (vs humility)

  • The human drivers do not change

  • Humans spend a lot of money to signal to other humans that they are "fit" (your DNA is great and your offspring will be fantastic)

  • Luxury goods
  • In the real world, it's through clothes, the restaurants you go to (that's one of the values of Instagram)
  • NFTs v1 can solve the same need (e.g., the Bored Ape)

  • NFTs v2: NFTs are a tech solution to the fact that your most important possessions are all digital (e.g., photos, an entry in a DB to represent that you went to Berkeley)

  • Product-market fit

  • = you have something that is so excellent that the market is going to pull it out of you
  • = a product that the market demands so much that the builders of the product will succeed despite their best efforts to fail
  • E.g., Twitter (they can barely keep the website up and they are worth $40B)

  • Success is easy if you have product-market fit

  • "Why Now?" is the most important question

  • Markets are pretty efficients and they prevent a certain innovation from succeeding / existing for a reason 1) New technology
  • E.g., battery technology enabled electric cars 2) New user acquisition channel
  • E.g., search / SEO
  • Tokenomics 3) New business model
  • Advertising supports free content online 4) Customer behavior has shifted
  • People understand the consequences of permanent identity online -> ephemerality
  • Put your information online to make it searchable by others -> social networking 5) New regulation

  • Obamacare

  • How to do product validation?

  • Deeply understand your market
  • Deeply understand your user / human need
  • Learn (aka fail) as quickly as possible
  • The company that moves is the one that moves faster

  • That's why startups win, it's because they can move and fail faster

  • People think that success is a straight line

  • In reality success is full of wrong turns

  • It's like failing all the times and feels terrible

  • Founder-product and founder-market fit

  • Because running a startup feels terrible, it's important that the founder has certain characteristics
  • E.g., the best products are created by people who are obsessed with the problem, the solution, the market and NOT with the outcome

  • It needs to be the mission of your life

  • Of the millions of people who could build this, why is it you that will build it?

  • Of the millions of products you could build, why is this the only product that your life should be dedicated to?
  • E.g., Elon Musk is obsessed with space

docs.text:
• Moonshot vs a sure-win
  • Moonshot = try to solve a problem that is kind of crazy, but if it works it's going to be absolutely massive

  • Sure win = it's not a revolutionary idea but it's good business

  • Startup returns are distributed as power-law

  • Almost all the returns come from the moonshot successes

  • The failure rate for moonshot are extremely high

  • If you build a moonshot, people (talent and VCs) are excited and energized

  • Moonshots builds gravitational pull
  • Amazon: "people are going to buy everything on-line"
  • Solana: "the fastest blockchain"
  • OpenSea: NFTs were illiquid, create market to increase a liquidity for NFTs

  • Uniswap: create best way to trade tokens

  • Sure things are not "venture scale"

  • VCs want to invest in moonshots

  • "X on Y" startup ideas (e.g., "Uber in Argentina", "OpenSea for Cardano")

  • Moonshot: "do something nobody is doing"
  • X on Y: "do something somewhere no one else is doing it"

  • Because of the efficient market hypothesis (EMH), either X or Y is small otherwise somebody would have already done it

  • Legacy companies lose to startups all the time

  • Retail: Amazon vs Walmart
  • Automotive: Tesla vs GM
  • Media: Facebook / YouTube vs Fox

  • Hospitality: Airbnb vs Marriott

  • When you change the technology, you also need to change the human organization

  • E.g., for a Web3 CEO needs to be technical, COO is the one talking about money

  • Startups build the organization from the ground up to match the new needs

  • Flywheel of innovation

  • A solution starts off as a "worse" solution to a problem

  • Infrastructure

  • Killer apps
  • User growth
  • Capital and founders

  • -> Investment in infrastructure (e.g., L2)

  • Then the flywheel is kicked off and it reaches escape velocity and unstoppable feedback loop

docs.title: Types of Investors: Angels, VCs, Accelerators
Pitching to Investors
docs.text:
• Startup founders are pitching all the times
  • To fund raise
  • To employees

  • To partners

  • Before the meeting

  • Try to build a relationship before pitching
  • Fundraising should not be the first interaction
  • Always try to get a warm intro
  • Much higher conversion rate
  • Investors rarely take cold meetings
  • Crypto VCs even less since industry is full of noise, BS artist, scammers

  • Use social proof (I went to Berkeley, I've worked with ...)

  • VCs get tons of emails

  • You need to cut through the noise

  • If you must go cold, try to engage

  • "I've read your Twitter", "I've read your paper"

  • Give enough personalization so it doesn't look like mass email

  • Canvas all the funds that could be a fit for your startup

  • There are DBs with principals, what they invest in, ...

  • Have an idea of who are prospective investors

  • Look at their portfolios, Crunchbase history

  • Most investors have specialization in certain areas

  • How to ask for a warm intro

  • Be direct
  • E.g., I'm doing this and that, can you do an intro for XYZ?"
  • Always provide a blurb (something you can copy-paste, don't play yourself up too much)
  • Intros are typically double opt-in
  • You ask for an intro
  • The person sends the blurb, asks if it's ok to do an intro
  • Do the intro
  • The more high-profile the person, the busier it is
  • Don't get upset if somebody doesn't respond
  • Try to keep meeting them
  • The introduction is like "this person is an awesome guy, you should chat with him"

  • Even VCs try to get intro to founders

  • Practice pitch with friends / advisors

  • Get honest feedback is difficult
  • Most people don't like to tell you that things are bad
  • Ask them to be super mean, pick on everything, be tough
  • Pitch on video (self-Zoom)
  • Wait a day to forget what you did!
  • Critique yourself

  • Take notes and improve

  • Prepare your deck and materials

  • Pretty much any presentation requires a deck

  • For a seed round

  • Tell a story in your deck
  • Narrative is everything
  • What are you going to build?

  • Why it's going to be huge?

  • Keep it short (shorter than you think, e.g., 10 slides)

  • A good idea is simple to explain

  • Keep slides simple and uncluttered

  • Avoid wall of text, too much fine print

  • The deck is not your pitch

  • It's just a visual aid / tool to augment your pitch

  • It should help to structure your pitch

  • Build your deck as if your audience is stupid and easily distracted

  • Very easy language

  • Avoid context dependence for each slide (people fall asleep and wake up)

  • Don't spend time explaining how cool crypto is

  • If you are pitching them, they should already be on-board

  • Five things to convey

  • Who you are

    • In a seed round, VCs invest in the founders and the team
  • What you do
    • It shouldn't take 5 slides to set the context to explain what you are doing
  • Why your startup will work
    • What's your edge
  • Why it'll change everything
    • Why is it going to be a good deal?

  • What you want from me

    • How much you want to raise?
    • Be direct

  • Things you don't need to convey

  • In a seed round, you don't need a monetization plan or token model
  • The focus is "are you going to build something valuable?"

  • How to extract value comes later

  • A valuation

  • You need to know how much you are raising

  • The market usually determines the valuation

  • A TAM

  • Mostly TAM calculations in crypto are BS, it's just difficult to estimate

  • The actual pitch

  • Do not just read through your deck!
  • Deck is a visual aid to amplify what you are saying
  • You are not narrating your deck, you need to show who you are

  • Feel free to skip slides, run quickly

  • The point of a pitch is to persuade the investor, not to cover the pitch

  • Don't try to impress with technical jargon

  • Over-complication dazzle investors
  • High-quality investors assume you can explain complicated concepts in a simple way

  • If you can't do it, you won't be able to do it to customers, employees

  • Use charts and diagrams, make them simple

  • If the deck requires attention to parse and decipher, it's distracting away from you, instead of being a visual aid

  • Make your pitch as clear as possible

  • Teach the investors, don't just try to impress

  • Sell your vision

  • Project enthusiasm, excitement

  • Show that you are the founder that can do it

  • Pulling a round together

  • You want to look busy and you are in high-demand
  • Signalling is half the game
  • Investors are monkeys:
  • "Do you want this? Yes? I want it too"
  • Something wants to talk
  • Saying "I'm free all day" is bad

  • I'm busy but I have a couple of slides

  • Build the impression of scarcity

  • "I'm chatting with a lot of investors"
  • "Allocation in your round might be tight"

  • "My round is in high demand, you better act quickly"

  • A lack of choosiness signals a lack of demand or a lack of experience

  • If you promise someone something, your word should be ironclad

  • Investors talk
  • Reputations last a long time

  • When you are a founder, you are in the big league

  • Unless you make a promise or sign a term sheet (not binding but a gentlemen agreement), everything is preliminary

  • People can be upset (for the right or the wrong reasons)

  • Think in terms a pipeline

  • Reach out to investors you are less excited about first
  • Get some pitching reps in
  • Then go after the dream team

  • Contact slower-moving investors first (bigger, older firms)

  • "I can't give you a response right now, but I will be able to in X days"

  • Be in control of the process

  • Pursue a strong lead

  • A strong lead takes at least half a round
  • The strong lead set the terms and the valuation

  • The opposite is a party round (the responsibility to support you is diluted)

  • A party round with small funds might be ok, since everybody is working hard

  • How much you need to spend and to raise

  • Every time you have a zero-sum decision, it's a negotiation point

  • You need to always show strength

  • Usually it takes 2-3 meetings to get to a term sheet

  • Angels can do more work pound for pound than a big VC would do

  • Sometimes angels are pain in the neck

  • Valuation

  • Founders want to maximize valuation (since it means less dilution for the money they give you)

  • Vast majority of the startup (98-99%) doesn't see a value

  • Almost always the VC that gives you the highest valuation is not the best VC to maximize the chances of success

  • Valuation is not a grade, but it is a tool to maximize your changes of success

  • It is super important to get the right persons at the table

  • Once terms are in sight, you need to introduce deadlines and get things moving

  • Otherwise investors assume they can wait
  • Founders need to prod and get things closed

docs.title: Ethics and Social Responsibility in Tech
Regulatory Framework and Compliance
docs.text:
• Basics of regulations
  • Rules that:
  • prohibit conduct (e.g., robbery) or

  • condition it on compliance with certain obligations (e.g., activities that you can carry out but you need to follow certain practices)

  • Why do we need regulations?

  • The belief is "The market cannot be left to its own devices"
  • Reduce market power (e.g., monopolies)
  • Facilitate competition (e.g., markets are open and new firms can enter and challenge the incompetents)
  • Promote stability
  • Attract investments
  • Protect consumers

  • Achieve governmental interests

  • Who makes and enforces

  • US has regulations on both state and federal levels
  • There are 3 branches of Government
  • Legislature branch (Congress) make laws
  • Executive enforces laws

  • Judiciary interprets laws

  • Securities laws

  • SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) goals are:
  • protect investors
  • facilitate capital formation

  • maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets

  • In 1920 ("the roaring 20s") there was a huge bubble of:

  • Financial abuse
  • Information asymmetry (e.g., issuers of financial instruments vs purchasers)

  • Federal securities laws originated in 1930 after the Great Depression

  • SEC regulates securities and market actors (e.g., issuers, exchanges, advisers, brokers, dealers, investment firms)

  • Crypto and securities laws

  • Registered securities are subject to onerous requirements
  • E.g., traded on SEC-regulated venues, held by SEC-approved custodians
  • Designation of a digital asset as a security is a death blow

  • Crypto industry spends time and money to avoid SEC regulation

  • Anti-Money Laundering Laws

  • Global framework for detecting and preventing criminals from using financial systems
  • The focus is on financial intermediaries (e.g., bank, casino), you need to do KYC (Know-Your-Customers), e.g., understand source and purpose of transactions and report it to the Government
  • The government doesn't have enough resources to monitor transactions, so it delegates this to intermediaries turning them into government agencies
  • The problem is that crypto replace all intermediaries with code
  • This still allows someone to monitor transactions but it's a big shift for the government
  • Money transmitter = entity that takes custody of customer funds to keep safe or to transmit
  • E.g., Coinbase, Kraken, PayPal
  • They are all regulated and need to do KYC

docs.title: 1, What the Heck Is EOS?
docs.text:
• EOS
  • Entrepreneurial Operating System
  • = the way a company organizes all of its human energy to
  • Solve problems
  • Meet
  • Plan
  • Prioritize
  • Communicate
  • Clarify roles
  • Lead

  • Manage

  • Inconsistency in company operating systems leads to

  • Poor communication
  • Dysfunction
  • Employees feeling frustrated and confused about the priorities

  • The company not realizing its full potential

  • If everyone does things in their own way the organization can't work

  • Meet when they want
  • Set their priorities

  • Use different terminology

  • When people move from project to project

  • A new system needs to be learned
  • Different way of reporting status updates

  • New way to run meetings

  • Why EOS?

  • Designed for 10-250 person companies
  • Need to be open-minded and growth-oriented
  • More than 50k companies run on EOS
  • EOS is simple and complete and helps companies grow and achieve goals / vision
  • Everybody is rowing in the same direction
  • Eliminate time-wasting actives due to miscommunication

  • EOS saves time

  • What's in It for Me?

  • EOS helps you
  • Work more effectively
  • Less frustration
  • Clear understanding of connection between your efforts and success of the company

docs.title: 2, How Does EOS Work?
docs.text:
• 6 Key Components of a Company on EOS
  • Every company is comprised of 6 key components
  • Vision
  • People
  • Data
  • Issues
  • Process

  • Traction

  • EOS requires open and honest communication

  • The Vision Component

  • Goal is to have everyone move in the same direction so that energy is not wasted
  • Avoid running around in circles, make the same mistakes over and over
  • More gets done in less time

  • Work is more fun

  • Tools for Vision Component

  • Vision/Tracker Organizer (VTO) is the tool to keep everyone in the company aligned on the same short / long term goals
  • It requires to answer 8 questions

  • Make sure the company agrees and buys in to the answers of the 8 questions

  • The People Component

  • You need to put "the right people in the right seats"
  • Persons who consistently excels at a clearly defined, necessary job in the organization
  • When the company has 100% of the Right people in the Right seats
  • Work is done more efficiently
  • There are fewer fires to put out
  • Mistakes are rare
  • Communication is better

  • The Company is truly a great place to work

  • The Right People

  • The "right people" are:
  • The ones who just fit
  • People you like to work with
  • People who want to accomplish something every day
  • They sacrifice so that the team

  • They act according to the company's core values

  • The Right Seats

  • The "right seats" are the roles needed to best contribute to the organization

  • Tools for People Component

  • Accountability Chart

  • People Analyzer

  • To answer the questions

  • Am I right person for this Company?
  • Do I fit?
  • Am I in the right seat?

  • Can I do my job really well?

  • The Data Component

  • Many companies fly blind all the time, like a plane with no gauges and no radar

  • Tools for Data Component

  • Scorecards
  • Handful of numbers (i.e., Measurables) that tell you how you are doing and where you are going
  • Each department and team should have a Scorecard
  • Measurables
  • One person should be accountable for each of it
  • E.g.,
    • Customer sale meetings
    • Units produced
  • Each person should have a Measurable and a goal for that number
  • Pros
  • You know how you are doing
  • Your manager knows what you have accomplished
  • The team can see if you are on track

  • You can find problems become a crisis

  • The Issue Component

  • Issues are things that can be improved, fixed, or changed to make your company better, e.g.,
  • Anything unresolved that needs to be discussed
  • Problems
  • Opportunities
  • New and better ways of doing things
  • E.g.,
  • Sell more
  • Reduce rework

  • Fix inventory problems

  • Seeing problems but not solving them leads to finger-pointing, dysfunction, frustration on both managers and employees

  • Everybody role is to bring up issues as they see them and help solve them

  • Tools for Issue Component

  • Issues list
  • Allow everyone to openly and honestly list all unresolved issues
  • Issues solving track

  • Disciplined way to help prioritize and solve issues

  • The Process Component

  • Create at a high level a consistent way of doing all the company's operations, e.g.,
  • All the projects are managed in the same way
  • How you make your product or service
  • How salespeople sell your product (from generating leads to closing the deals)
  • How to serve your customers so that they are always satisfied

  • How the Company bills and collects money

  • Following the same process:

  • Saves an incredible amount of time
  • Eliminates frustration

  • Help to perform the job with fewer mistakes and delays

  • Everyone follows the processes, creating consistency and efficiency

  • Using processes the company can grow and scale in a manageable way

  • Once all processes for repetitious tasks are uniform, energy can be put to creative tasks and solve the unexpected

  • The Traction Component

  • In a company with no traction

  • People in your company are not accountable
  • Things don't get done on time
  • Due dates are constantly missed

  • Your Company takes on too much

  • The goal of the Traction component is to:

  • Get projects completed on time
  • People who commit to a deadline hit it
  • People put the extra effort needed and don't want to let one another down
  • People can't make excuses for being unproductive and so leave

  • Everyone focuses on only a few priorities for the next 90 days (which are tied to the company's overall goals)

  • Tools for the Traction Component

  • Rocks
  • Most important things that need to get done in the next 90 days
  • Level 10 meetings
  • Have an agenda
  • Solve issues

  • Allow the team to stay connected

  • Summary

Component What's it all about Tool(s) Your Role Vision Getting everyone aligned and focused on the same vision V/TO Understand and buy into the answers to the 8 V/TO questions People Getting the Right People in the Right Seats Accountability Chart, People Analyzer Ask yourself if you are the Right Person in the Right Seat Data Measuring performance and having a pulse Scorecard, Measurables Establish and achieve your Measurables Issues Identifying and solving issues Issues List, Issues Solving Track Bring up and help solve issues Process Documenting the way you do things and being consistent Documented Core Process Learn, follow, and help improve the Core Processes Traction Accountability, discipline, and execution Meeting Pulse, Rocks Complete your Rocks and engage in meetings

docs.title: 3, Do You See What They Are Saying?
docs.text:
• The Vision
  • Every Company should have a crystal clear vision, which is written down and shared with everyone
  • Only in this way every one rows in the same direction

  • Otherwise there is poor communication, confusion, wasted effort

  • Sometimes

  • Leaders carry the vision in their heads

  • Leaders believe everyone agree on the same vision, and they really don't

  • V/TO

  • Vision/Traction Organizer
  • The goal is have a shared map the for where the Company has been, is, and is going
V/TO Question What it answers Core Values Who you are Core Focus What you are 10-Year Target Where you are going Marketing Strategy Which potential customers you are targeting with what message 3-Year Picture What you will look like in 3 years 1-Year Plan What your goals are for the next 12 months Rocks What your priorities are for the next 90 days Issues What will stop you or get you there faster
  • V/TO 1: What Are Your Core Values?
  • Core values
  • Are a timeless set of guiding principles
  • Define the culture, who fits and who doesn't

  • Define what makes the Company different and unique

  • In a Company, culture wins in the long term

  • A Company needs to know who it is

  • If people share the core values

  • Core Values: Examples

  • Be humble but confident
  • Grow or die
  • Help first
  • Do what you say
  • E.g., if you commit to a date, you hit it
  • You fully deliver and finish what you start: no half-assed things
  • If you can't do it, don't commit

  • Do the right thing

  • V/TO 2: What Is Your Core Focus?

  • Core Focus is about:
  • Keeping your company focused on the areas where your business excels

  • Not getting distracted by the "shiny stuff"

  • You can't be everything to everyone

  • You need to have a Niche: something you do better than anyone else

  • V/TO 3: What Is Your 10-Year Target?

  • 10-Year Target
  • Is your long-term, larger-than-life goal

  • Unites everyone around one common objective

  • V/TO 4: What Is Your Marketing Strategy?

  • Clarify
  • Who your ideal customer is

  • The most appealing message to them

  • Then laser-focus on it and do now waste money and effort

  • Trying to be everting to everyone
  • With inconsistent marketing message
  • Taking trips to prospective customers who are not a good fit for the company or are not going to say yes

  • Committing to projects in which they don't have expertise

  • Marketing Strategy

  • It has 4 key elements
  • Target market
    • Characteristics of your best customers
    • E.g., who they are, where they are, how they think
    • Focus on customers who is best to do business with
    • E.g.,
    • $5-50M in revenue
    • 20-250 employees
    • Southeastern US
    • Growth-oriented
    • Seeking a partner, not a commodity provider
  • 3 Uniques
    • Things that make you better than the competition and why your customers should buy from you
    • Consistent messaging market for sales and marketing efforts
    • E.g.,
    • 99% on-time delivery
    • Local technicians
    • 24hr response time
  • Proven process
    • A visual of what you do to deliver value to your customers
    • What your customers will experience working with you

  • Guarantee

    • It says you stand behind your product or service
    • Put your clients at ease
    • E.g.,
    • "We will hit our ship date, or will pay for shipping"
    • "If we don't add value, you don't pay"
    • "We will show up on time, or the first hour is free"

  • V/TO 5: What Is Your 3-Year Picture?

  • Paint a picture of what your company will look like in 3 years
  • Revenue
  • Profit
  • A Measurable

  • 5-10 bullets to paint a vivid image of what your Company will look like, feel like, be like in 3 years

  • E.g.,

  • Revenue: $15m
  • Profit: $2m
  • Measurable: 300 customers

  • What does it look like?

    • 80 employees
    • 3 new product lines
    • 100% Right people in the Right seats
    • Strong culture
    • Largest customer accounts for <10% of revenue
    • All Core processes documented and followed by all

  • It needs to be written down and shared with everyone

  • V/TO 6: What Is Your 1-Year Plan?

  • Revenue target
  • Profit target
  • Measurable
  • Top 3-7 goals for the year
  • Fewer is better

  • With too many things to do, people lose focus and accomplish very few of them

  • This will put you on a path to reach the 3-year picture and the 10-year target

  • V/TO 7: What Are Your Rocks?

  • Rocks are the 3-7 most important objectives the company must get done in the next 90 days (i.e., one quarter) to achieve the 1-year plan

  • The 90 days is to keep people focused and energetic on the priorities

  • There are always unplanned emergencies, day-to-day distractions
  • Then plans start to unravel

  • You need to break the overall goals into smaller and manageable chunks

  • After 90 days, you start losing focus and new set of Rocks will refocus the Company

  • V/TO 8: What Are Your Company's Issues?

  • To achieve the vision you need to admit all of your company's obstacles, everything that can prevent the company from reaching your vision

  • Every company has issues

  • No one admits them
  • Everyone might talk about it but does nothing

docs.title: 4, Who's Doing What?
docs.text:
• Without Roles and Responsibilities
  • In an organization where roles and responsibilities are unclear
  • People trip over each other
  • Everyone is working hard but running in circles
  • Accomplish very little

  • Finger-pointing

  • The right structure will:

  • Clarify roles and responsibilities
  • Create clear reporting lines
  • Facilitate efficient decision making
  • Help people get things done
  • Enable communication

  • Identity all the available seats in the organization

  • Accountability

  • All-for-one-and-for-all approach works only for small (< 10 people) startups

  • People wear many hats to keep the company survive

  • As a Company mature, the all-for-one approach becomes a roadblock to growth

  • People trip over each other
  • Everyone is still trying to do everything
  • Company stalls
  • Pressure and stress increase

  • The blame game starts

  • No one knows who is responsible for what

  • No one is held accountable for anything

  • There are too many cooks in the kitchen

  • You miss a customer deadline

  • Everyone points fingers

  • You lose a major customer

  • 4 different people have 4 different explanations of what happened

  • When everyone is accountable, no one is

  • The Accountability chart

  • It is an organizational chart that
  • Shows structure
  • Clarifies the roles and responsibilities (the "seat")
    • Five bullet points explaining
  • No confusing reporting lines from an employee to multiple bosses

  • Establishes clear ownership and accountability for everything

  • There is no "right" accountability chart because every company is different

  • The accountability chart is specific of your company based on size, growth goals, culture, product, or service

  • The Accountability Chart: Example

docs.title: Organizational Chart: Example
docs.text:
• An example of organizational chart is: ``` ## Visionary Sally M.
  • Big Ideas
  • Big Relationships
  • Culture
  • Industry Trends

## Integrator Robert D. - LMA* - Achieve Budget - Legal - Special Projects

## Finance John P. - Reporting - Accounting - Cash

### HR Chrissi L. - HR Process - Finding Candidates - Benefits - Review Process

### IT Dana G. - Systems - Computers - Internet - Phones

### Accounting John L. - AP - AR - Expenses

## Operations James Z. - LMA* - Client Satisfaction - Manage Resources - Ops Process

### Field Tech 7 People - Product Delivery - Solve Client Problems - Customer Service

### Sales Rep 2 People - New Biz Dev - Hit Goals - Pipeline

## Sales Mary S. - LMA* - Revenue - Sales Process / Selling - Manage Clients

## Marketing David S. - Branding - Generate Leads - Website

  • LMA = Leadership, Management, Accountability ```

  • Scalability and Evolution

  • The same seat can be filled by multiple people performing the same function
  • Ability to adjust is critical
  • The accountability chart may change every quarter / 90 days

  • People might change seat or leave

  • Communication

  • Communication should flow across all lines and departments
  • Create an open and honest culture
  • Avoid silos

docs.title: 5, What Is Most Important Right Now?
docs.text:
• Rocks: Intuition
  • You have a small pile of rocks, some pebbles, and some sand
  • Your objective is to fit them all in a glass jar
  • If you put the sand first and then the pebbles, the rocks don't fit

  • If you put the rocks first and then the pebbles and the sand (which filters through the bigger things), it fits

  • Rocks

  • The rocks represent the most important things you must get done
  • The pebbles are your day-to-day responsibilities

  • The sand represents all the interruptions during the day

  • If you don't prioritize your Rocks (the most important things first), you will not get them done

  • The 90-Day World

  • Human mind tends to lose focus

  • Every 90 days

  • you get together with your team
  • review the Rocks that were accomplished

  • Set the Rocks for the next 90 days

  • Everything else (things you don't have capacity, things that are not as important) is pushed to the next period, minimizing wasted effort, talking too much

  • The problem:

  • Work on a project for a few weeks
  • The manager says that it wasn't a priority any more

  • Assign a new project

  • Your Rocks

  • Each individual should have 1-3 Rocks every 90 days
  • Rocks should be aligned with your company or your team's Rocks
  • E.g.,
    • If your team Rock is "Purchase 4 new trucks"
    • Your Rock could be "Find 10 potential trucks to buy that match the needed specification"
  • Rocks should be tied to your day-to-day responsibilities

  • E.g., for a salesperson the Rock is "schedule 20 sales appointments"

  • SMART

  • Each Rock needs to be SMART
  • Specific
    • Is it clear enough?
  • Measurable
    • Can you measure (with a number) the completion of your Rock?
  • Attainable
    • Can you achieve it?
  • Realistic
    • Can you complete the Rock in 90 days?

  • Timely

    • Is this the right time?

  • SMART vs non-SMART Rocks

  • Bad: Safety inspection

  • Good: Pass 100% of safety inspections

  • Bad: Online class

  • Good: Successfully complete an online training class on website marketing

  • Reviewing Rocks Weekly

  • You need to check on the team during weekly meetings
  • Every team needs to report if the team is "on track" or "off track"
  • This creates a new language to hold people accountable

  • People should not take it personally

  • Completing 80% of the Rocks every 90 days is a great job

docs.title: 6, Why Do We Have to Have Meetings?
docs.text:
• Meetings
  • Meetings are not a waste of time

  • It's what you do in meetings that's a waste of time

  • Meeting should start and end on time

  • Provide input on which issues to tackle

  • Participate in the decisions and the solutions

  • Meetings are necessary

  • How to End Procrastination

  • Human beings by nature procrastinate

  • Wait until the last minute to get things done

  • To solve procrastination you need to give a "pulse" to the organization

  • Weekly Meeting Pulse

  • EOS recommends a weekly meeting pulse

  • Since there is a spike of activity more often, there is no time to procrastinate

  • The goal is

  • Minimize number and length of meetings

  • Maximize meeting productivity

  • The "right meeting pulse" is to accomplish 4 things

  • Make sure everything is on track
  • Keep the team connected
  • Hold each other accountable

  • Solve issues

  • The meeting

  • Is always on the same day and same time
  • Starts and ends on time

  • Is 90 mins long

  • Level 10 Meetings

  • Roles in L10 Meetings

  • Meeting facilitator:
  • Runs the meeting
  • Move the team through the agenda
  • Keep everything on track
  • Scribe:
  • Bring the list of Rocks, Scorecard, Agenda
  • Update the documents
  • There should be two different persons

  • It's difficult to play both roles

  • L10 Agenda

  • Wins / good news (5 mins)
  • Scorecard (5 mins)
  • Rocks review (5 mins)
  • Customer / employee headlines (5 mins)
  • Todo list (5 mins)
  • ...
  • Identity-discuss-solve (60 mins)
  • ...

  • Conclusion (5 min)

  • Wins

  • Each person shares one piece of good news from the past week
  • Help humanize the process
  • Allow team members to get to know each other

  • Start the meeting off with a positive vibe

  • Scorecard

  • Make sure your Measurables (KPIs, metrics) are on track
  • You should just review, no questions, no commentary, no excuses
  • You either hit the goal for the week or you didn't
  • There is no discussion
  • Any comment is dropped won to the Issues List
  • Simply say "Drop it down"

  • You want to avoid a painful reporting session of why and how the numbers are bad

  • Rock Review

  • Make sure that each person's Rocks are on track
  • The facilitator reads the list of Rocks one at a time

  • The Rock owner states if it's on track or not

    • No questions, no commentary, now excuses
    • Any question needs to get dropped down to the Issues List

  • It takes discipline

  • Customer / Employee Headlines

  • Everyone can bring up good or bad news about customers, employees, or both
  • 1-2 sentence headline

  • If it takes more, drop it down

  • TODOs

  • These are the commitments made by people in the last L10 meeting
  • If something was off-track last week, it was decided to be fixed

  • Was it done?

  • TODOs are 7 day action items

  • The goal is to complete 90% of them each week

  • IDS

  • This is were you solve all your key issues

  • You are going to have 60 mins to solve the issues

  • There are 3 types of issues

  • Decisions
    • E.g., "customer XYZ is not happy with the level of customer support"
  • Information to share
    • E.g., "we are having our 2 largest customers into the office this week"

  • Information is needed

    • E.g., "Roger needs to know when the next software release will be"

  • The goal is to

  • solve the most important issues well (so they don't come back!)

  • not to solve all the issues on your list

  • If you run out of time, the other issues can stay on the list until next week

  • IDS

  • IDS is the issues solving tracking tool
  • Identify
  • Discuss

  • Solve

  • Meetings are a waste of time if teams spend all their time discussing an issue

  • They just talk and talk and feel productive

  • You need to clearly identify the issue

  • Who, Who, 1-Sentence

  • To clearly identify the issue
  • Who: is raising the issue
  • Who: is accountable for solving the issue

  • 1-sentence: state the issue in one sentence by stating the problem directly to her (short, sweet, no candy-coating)

  • Bob tells Sue "I'm not getting reports from you on time"

  • Then there is a productive conversation about the problem and how to solve it

  • Tangent Alert

  • People start getting off the subject and going down rabbit holes

  • Simple say "tangent alert!"

  • Conclusion

  • With 5 mins left in the meeting, even if you are in the middle of an issue, you need to do 3 things to end the meeting on time

  • Recap the todo list

  • Decide if there are important messages to communicate inside / outside the company based on the decisions you have made

  • Rate the meting

  • Rate the Meeting

  • Did it start and end on time?
  • Did you follow the L10 agenda?
  • Is everyone on the same page?
  • Did 90% or more of the todos get done?

  • Did you solve the most important issues?

  • The minimum average rating should be 8

  • If somebody ranks the meeting below an 8 you should ask "what would have made the meeting a 10 for you?"
  • Collect answers on how to improve

docs.title: 7, What's My Number?
docs.text:
• Without a Scorecard
  • Companies work hard but don't know how they are doing
  • People
  • Are frustrated
  • Are unmotivated
  • Perform poorly
  • The result is:
  • Wasted time
  • Poor resource allocation
  • Weak overall performance

  • Terrible results

  • The Scorecard

  • The Scorecard:
  • Is a handful of numbers that how the company or your department are doing
  • Tells what is working and what is not
  • Solves issues before they become major disasters
  • Eliminate assumptions and egos

  • Creates transparency, accountability

  • Effect of the Scorecard

  • Everybody knows exactly where they are
  • Numbers are reviewed and tracked weekly
  • Everybody is constantly striving to hit their target
  • If people go off track, within one week the problem is discussed as IDS and fixed

  • Everybody is accountable

  • "What gets measure gets done"

  • "If you shoot for the moon, you get to where nobody else can reach"

  • A Typical Scorecard

  • The Company has a scorecard with 5-15 numbers

  • Each department has a scorecard with 3-5 numbers

  • All scorecards for Company and Departments are reviewed weekly in the L10 meeting

  • Usually you want to produce current activity that produces future results, e.g.,

  • Utilization
  • Number of sales meetings
  • Average time to resolve complaints

  • Number of bugs fixed

  • Each activity should be tied to future results, such as revenues, sales, and profits

  • E.g., achieve $10M in revenue
  • 5 new clients per week, which is $200,000 in sales per week

  • You need to schedule 20 sales meetings per week

  • Scorecards: Columns

  • Each scorecard should have 4 key columns
  • Who: person accountable for the number
    • The person who can most influence the number
    • Not the one who reports (e.g., a manager)
  • Measurables: 3-5 numbers
  • Goal: the number that must be hit every week

  • Date: week we are reporting for

  • Everyone's Number

  • Everyone should have a number
  • A number
  • Cuts through the subjective communication
  • Creates accountability
    • Expectations are clear
  • Creates commitment
  • Creates competition
  • Creates the right kind of pressure and peer-pressure
  • Produce results
  • Solves problem faster
    • If an activity is off track, the problem can be recognized and solved
  • Right people in the right seats appreciate numbers
  • "Wrong people in the wrong seats resist Measurables"

docs.title: 8, How Am I Doing?
docs.text:
• Right People in the Right Seats

  • Great organizations are built by having 100% "the Right people in the Right seats"

  • Right people are the ones who fit in the Company's culture and share the Core Values

  • People should have job where their innate talents and skills are put to the best use

  • Each seat has 5 roles and responsibilities, e.g.,

  • Solve customer issues
  • Document customer interactions
  • Escalate when appropriate

  • ...

  • People Analyzer: Step 1

  • For each person you need to rate how they do with respect to Company's Core Values
  • Match the Core Values
  • +: most of the time
  • +/-: sometimes

  • -: rarely

  • Then you need to set "the bar", i.e., the minimum acceptable score to accept

  • Recommended 3 + and 2 +/-

  • People Analyzer: Step 2

  • You can use 3 criteria called "GWC" to understand if each person is in the Right Seat

  • Do they get the job?

  • Do they understand all the ins and outs of the position?
  • Do they understand how their job relates to the other jobs?
  • Are they "wired" for that job?

  • E.g., a flight attendants who is rude, a salesperson who don't understand the product after months of training

  • Do they want the job?

  • Do they get up every morning wanting to do the job?

  • Do they show passion for it?

  • Do they have the capacity to do the job?

  • Do they have the ability and the time to do the job?

  • E.g., a pest-control field rep who is scared of bugs

  • For these questions there are only yes or no, no maybes

  • The bar is 3 yeses

  • People Analyzer: Step 3

  • Apply the People Analyzer to yourself and your seat

  • You need to be completely honest and open

  • Sometimes the problem is just being in the wrong seat

  • People are often unhappy when in the wrong seat

  • The Quarterly Conversation

  • Employees often report that they would love more feedback and opportunities to discuss how they are doing

  • Every manager should have a quarterly conversation with their direct reports

  • You should compare notes

  • You can use the People Analyzer
  • It should not be a blame session

  • Everybody has things that are not working and can be improved

  • Informal 1-hour one-on-one meeting to

  • Talk about what's working and what's not
  • Clarify expectations
  • Communicate well

  • Make course corrections

  • Questions About What Works

  • What am I most proud of accomplishing in the last quarter?
  • What changes did I make to accomplish my job?
  • What did I do well to hit my Rocks and Measurables?
  • Am I working on projects and in a role that matters?

  • Do I demonstrate the Company's Core Values?

  • Questions About What Doesn'T Work

  • What makes my job more difficult?
  • What processes / procedures are broken?
  • What could I have done differently?
  • How could my manager help me being more successful?

  • What's not working?

  • A good or bad Annual Performance Review should never be a surprise

docs.title: 9, What Do I Do Next?
docs.text:
• Implementing EOS

  • Implementing EOS in your Company is a lifelong effort

  • We have a clear vision who is shared by everyone

  • Our core values are clear
  • We use our core values to hire, review, reward, and fire
  • Our Core Focus is clear
  • Our 10-year target is clear and shared
  • Our target market is clear and all marketing and sales efforts
  • Our 3 unique differentiators are clear
  • We have a proven process for doing business with our customers
  • All of the people in the Company are the "right people" (i.e., share our core values)
  • Our Accountability Chart is clear, completed, and constantly updated
  • Everyone is in the right seat
  • Everyone has Rocks and is focused on them
  • All meetings are on the same day / time, have the same agenda, start / end on time
  • Our Core Processes are documented and followed
  • We have systems for receiving regular feedback from customers and employees
  • A Scorecard for tracking weekly metrics / measurables is in place
  • We have a budget and are monitoring it regularly

docs.title: The Automated Solution
docs.text:
Our pipeline stitches together LinkedIn scraping, email validation, and campaign management into one flow:

LinkedIn → PhantomBuster → Email Validation → Campaign Launch

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
PhantomBuster: Your LinkedIn scraping engine - Connects to Sales Navigator searches - Pulls profile data automatically (no manual clicking) - Exports to structured data you can actually use - Handles rate limits so you don't get banned

Hunter.io + DropContact: The email-finding duo - Hunter.io: Finds emails using name + company domain - DropContact: Finds emails using just first/last name + company - Both verify email validity before you send - Combined approach catches 80%+ of valid emails

YAMM (Yet Another Mail Merge): Google Sheets email automation - Sends personalized emails directly from Google Sheets - Tracks opens, clicks, and responses automatically - Handles unsubscribes and bounces - No need for expensive email platforms

Google Sheets: The control center - Every step creates a new tab (search → filtered → emails → campaign) - Easy to review data at each stage - Non-technical team members can see progress - Built-in version control for different campaigns

docs.title: The Flow
docs.text:
1. Target Definition: Define your audience (VCs, customers, partners, employees, etc.)
  2. LinkedIn Extraction: Use Sales Navigator templates to pull relevant profiles
  3. Profile Filtering: Remove irrelevant contacts, keep only decision makers
  4. Email Discovery: Run profiles through Hunter.io and DropContact
  5. Email Validation: Filter out dead/invalid emails
  6. Campaign Launch: Send personalized messages via YAMM

docs.title: What You Get
docs.text:
• 20-50 verified contacts per target organization
  • Automated email validation (no bounces to hurt your domain)
  • Campaign tracking and response monitoring
  • Scalable process that works across any industry or role

docs.title: Data Sources We Tap
docs.text:
Beyond LinkedIn, we pull from:

  • Tracxn: Company data and investment patterns
  • Scrapes VC firm search results and portfolio companies
  • Extracts investor names, funding rounds, and sectors
  • Downloads as .mhtml files to bypass rate limiting

  • Provides investment history and decision-maker contacts

  • Signal NFX: Investor lists by stage and vertical

  • Curated lists of investors for different stages (pre-seed, seed, Series A)
  • Organized by vertical (AI, fintech, healthcare, etc.)
  • Extracts investor names and firm data from paginated lists

  • Handles dynamic loading to capture complete datasets

  • FolkApp: Professional profile data

  • Scrapes shared VC databases using Playwright automation
  • Handles virtualized tables with dynamic row loading
  • Extracts profile data, companies, and contact information

  • Processes structured data into clean CSV formats

  • Industry databases: Specialized prospect sources

  • Money2020: Conference attendee data with authenticated API access
  • Growjo: Fastest-growing companies by industry with revenue/funding data
  • Datamation: AI company listings with headquarters and revenue details
  • 50pros.com: Fortune 500 company data including CEOs and key personnel

Manual sources: Curated and verified data - Internal Google Sheets with verified contact information - Conference attendee lists from industry events - Manually researched and validated prospect databases - Team-contributed contact lists with quality control

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Fundraising: Find VCs, angels, and partners at target funds
  • Sales: Identify decision makers at target companies
  • Hiring: Source candidates with specific skill sets
  • Partnerships: Connect with business development teams
  • Customer research: Reach users in your target segments

docs.title: The Technical Reality
docs.text:
This isn't plug-and-play. You need: - API keys for each service - Google Sheets integration - Jupyter notebooks for customization - Data cleaning functions for each vertical

Bottom line: Manual outreach doesn't scale. Automation does. Build the pipeline once, run it forever.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Without systematic outreach, you're relying on warm intros and luck. With it, you can test messaging, track response rates, and iterate fast. The difference between 10 conversations and 100 conversations is the difference between hoping someone will respond and having evidence that they will.
